title: Not one stone (Luke 21:1–6)
hookLine: the widow's mites, then the Temple's beauty and its end
tomorrow: Do this for a commemoration of me

lines: THE CLINK OF RICH PEOPLE'S COINS.
cards: Two scenes sit side by side in Luke, within six verses, both in the Temple. In the first, Jesus watches rich people casting their gifts into the treasury, a steady clink of coins.
Then a poor widow drops in two brass mites. In the second, some people are admiring the building itself: its goodly stones, and the gifts that adorn it. A tiny gift, and a vast one.

teach.h: TWO BRASS MITES IN THE TREASURY.
teach.b: First the widow. The Douay calls her coins two brass mites; Luke's Greek calls them lepta, small coins.
Jesus says: "Verily I say to you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all." The others gave out of their abundance. She gave out of her want, all the living that she had.
Jesus doesn't measure the amount. He measures what was left after. Then, a moment later, people are praising the Temple.

teach.h: A TEMPLE LIKE A SNOWY MOUNTAIN.
teach.b: This was the Temple Herod the Great had rebuilt, and Josephus, who saw it, says that from a distance it looked like a snowy mountain, white stone and gold.

And Jesus says: "The days will come in which there shall not be left a stone upon a stone that shall not be thrown down." Yesterday he said it weeping, on the hill. Today he says it standing among the stones themselves.
Put the two scenes together and they ask one question: what lasts? The great stones, admired by the crowd, did not. The two coins, noticed by Jesus, are still read aloud wherever this Gospel is read.
Luke isn't saying buildings are bad. Catholics build cathedrals. He's asking where a heart rests.

teach.h: NOT A STONE UPON A STONE.
teach.b: A gift of the whole self is remembered.

how: Catholics bring offerings to the altar at the offertory of every Mass, and parishes sometimes point to the widow's mite when they speak of giving: not the size of the gift, but how much of yourself is in it.

games.q: you're standing in the Temple courts with your friends, admiring the enormous polished stones. Jesus is with you. what does he say?
o: it's the most beautiful building in the world.
not a stone will be left upon a stone.
give generously to keep it standing.
games.why: he says the days will come when not a stone upon a stone will remain, and the beautiful stones will be thrown down.

practice: Make a quiet list of what you're proud of, or worried about keeping, a house, a title, a reputation, a bank balance, and hold each one a moment as what it is: good, and temporary.

Then bring to mind something that lasts, a love you've given, a kindness someone still remembers, faith if you have it, and rest there. If you pray, offer God something small and whole, like the widow's two coins.

wordCard.voice: Mites. The Douay's word for the widow's two small coins, worth more to Jesus than the Temple's great stones. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: lepta, small coins. The Douay calls them mites.

carryVoice: Your line: what lasts. Two brass mites outlasted all the Temple's goodly stones. See you tomorrow.
